title: What is known about 1RB0RD_0LC1LD_1RA1LA_1RE1LB_---0RF_1RA1RF
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0RD_0LC1LD_1RA1LA_1RE1LB_---0RF_1RA1RF.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state machine halts from blank tape. This page describes what its run looks like at the level of words and counters, what a halt would need, and what is still missing. The description comes from simulation (first look, about an hour of study); nothing beyond the bounded runs is proved.
verdict: The question is open. Lean proves no halt in the first 107 steps, the C simulator none in 109. The macro structure described below is observed in the simulation, not proved.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (E0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: Where a halt can come from
claims.text: If the machine halts on its third step from a configuration, that configuration is one of: A with 1 under the head, 0 right, 0 two right. So a run can reach a halt only through one of these patterns, and a proof that the machine never halts only has to rule them out. The proof splits on the state and the five cells around the head.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 91,588 cells have been visited and 72,516 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: fixed/linear
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half). Right of the start it grows in proportion to the step count (the head drifts steadily that way) (fitted exponent 0.85).

claims.title: Full sweeps
claims.text: The head sweeps between the two ends of the tape; in 10<sup>8</sup> steps it reaches the right end in F 6,291 times and the left end 7,245 times (B or D).

claims.title: Square-root growth
claims.text: Width 2,000 at 1.5·10<sup>6</sup> steps, 16,000 at 8.4·10<sup>7</sup>: the width doubles when the time quadruples.

claims.title: Shift rules, for every n
claims.text: A crosses (1010)^n to the right and leaves (0101)^n; F crosses (0101)^n and leaves (1010)^n; for any tapes on both sides.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. No macro rule has been proved for this machine yet; see the README's Later section for the next steps.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows yet. The head sweeps an irregular word of short blocks back and forth; the word grows at both ends and the tape width grows like the square root of the time.

facts.text: tape width grows like the square root of the step count
No halt in the C simulator; 91,588 cells visited.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.

sections.heading: Full sweeps over an irregular word
html: The tape is a word of short blocks of 1s, each followed by a single 0, for example (step 93,864,904, from the left) 1 0 1^7 0 1^3 0 1 0 1 0 1 0 1^3 0 1 0 1^2 0 1 0 1^5 0 …. Long stretches are 1 0 1 0 …, the longer blocks have up to about 20 ones.

The head sweeps the whole word: in the first 108 steps it reaches the right end in state F 6,291 times and the left end in state B 3,656 times and in D 3,589 times. Most of the word is unchanged from one sweep to the next; the changes are near the two ends. The visited width roughly doubles each time the step count quadruples (2,000 cells at 1.5·106 steps, 4,000 at 5.9·106, 8,000 at 2.1·107, 16,000 at 8.4·107), so it grows like the square root of the time, as for a bouncer whose sweeps get longer by a constant.

sections.heading: What a halt would need
html: The machine halts when it reads a 0 in state E (E0 is the halting transition). E is entered from D on a 0 (D0 = 1RE); so a halt needs D>0 0, the head in D moving right onto two 0s in a row. In ten snapshots of the tape, one every 107 steps up to 108, there are no two adjacent 0s anywhere between the ends, so such a halt would have to happen at an end of the tape.

sections.heading: The sweep over the 1 0 stretches
html: The long 1 0 1 0 … stretches are crossed by two shift rules, proved for every length: A turns (1010)^n into (0101)^n, and F turns (0101)^n back. No exact map from one sweep to the next was found.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half). Right of the start it grows in proportion to the step count (the head drifts steadily that way) (fitted exponent 0.85).
After 109 steps the tape spans 91,588 cells (5,790 left of the start, 55,393 right), with a density of 1s of 0.792.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

family: two-ended sweeper over an irregular block word
summary: The head sweeps the whole tape back and forth; the tape is an irregular word of short blocks of 1s separated by single 0s, rewritten at both ends, and it grows like the square root of the step count.
